L5.1.quote: For $f(x)=x+c$ ($c\ge 0$) the original inequalities become $\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + (y+c)^2}{2}} \ge \frac{x+y+c}{2} \ge \sqrt{x(y+c)}$, which are exactly the Quadratic‑Mean–Arithmetic‑Mean inequality and the Arithmetic–Mean–Geometric‑Mean inequality applied to the two positive numbers $x$ and $y+c$. Both inequalities are true for all $x,y>0$.
L5.1.note: Full verification of both inequalities for all x, y and all c >= 0.

L5.2.quote: Put $x = f(y)$ (which is $>0$) in (2). ... Hence the chain collapses to equality: $(f(f(y)) + y)^2 = 4f(y)^2$. Taking square roots (all terms are positive) yields $f(f(y)) + y = 2f(y)$ $\Longrightarrow$ $f(f(x)) = 2f(x) - x$ $\forall x>0$.
L5.2.note: Correct sandwich argument at x = f(y); orbit AP via (4).

L5.3.note: Nowhere proves g(x) = f(x) - x >= 0; positivity-of-iterates argument absent, negative values of g never ruled out.

L5.4.quote: Take $n = qt$, $m = pt$ for $t\in\mathbb{N}$. ... For large $t$ the inequality is violated – contradiction. ... Then the right‑hand side of (9) tends to $0$ while the left‑hand side tends to $+\infty$, again a contradiction. Thus $V$ contains **at most one** positive number.
L5.4.note: Rational and irrational ratio cases both handled via iterate comparison in (9).

L5.5.quote: From (11) we immediately obtain $(x-y)^2 > c^2$, hence $|x-y| > c \;\forall x\in S_0, y\in S_c$. ... If $x \in S_0$, then by (12) we must have $|x - (u + n c)| > c$ (because $u+nc \in S_c$). This is impossible. Hence $S_0 = \emptyset$.
L5.5.note: Separation, Lemma 1, and covering argument are complete; but the premise V ⊆ {0,c} (i.e. f(x) ∈ {x, x+D}) rests on the unproven exclusion of negative g-values.
